artwork.title: Sleeping Hermaphroditus
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Jastrow, 2007, via Wikimedia Commons · public domain

lessons.title: A sleeper with two sides

n1.text: A figure sleeps face down, head resting on folded arms, on a marble mattress that looks soft enough to sink into.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Walk slowly round to the far side. This figure keeps a surprise that the near side does not show.

q1.text: What does the far side reveal?

choices.label: A body both male and female

correction.tempting: The mattress is wide enough for two.
correction.truth: The far side shows the figure's double nature: breasts and male genitals together.
correction.evidence: Galleria Borghese, Rome; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

b1b.text: Yes. From one side you see the back, the hips and the sleeping face. From the other, the figure is shown to be both female and male.

correction.tempting: The legs look tense, as if about to move.
correction.truth: The face suggests sleep. What the far side reveals is a body both female and male.
correction.evidence: Metropolitan Museum of Art; Galleria Borghese, Rome.

n2.text: This is Hermaphroditus, son of Hermes and Aphrodite. In Ovid's poem, the nymph Salmacis loved him and prayed never to be parted from him.

q2.text: How did the gods answer her prayer?

choices.label: They turned her into a spring

b2a.text: No: they changed his body, not its material.

correction.tempting: He lies as still as a stone.
correction.truth: The gods merged the two bodies into one being, both male and female.
correction.evidence: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

b2b.text: No: she was joined to him.

correction.tempting: The story takes place at a spring.
correction.truth: As he bathed, the gods merged the two bodies into one being, both male and female.
correction.evidence: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

b2c.text: Yes. The gods joined the nymph and Hermaphroditus into one new being, both male and female. The statue shows that being, asleep.

n3.text: The statue was dug up in Rome in the early 1600s and went to Cardinal Scipione Borghese. He asked the young Gian Lorenzo Bernini to give it a new base.

b3a.text: Yes. In 1620 Bernini carved the marble mattress and pillow. They seem to sink under the sleeper's weight.

b3b.text: The figure is ancient: it was dug up in Rome.

correction.tempting: The body is as finely carved as the mattress.
correction.truth: Bernini added the mattress and pillow in 1620; the figure is Roman.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

b3c.text: Not Bernini: he made the mattress and pillow.

correction.tempting: The face looks fresh and smooth.
correction.truth: Bernini carved the mattress and pillow in 1620; the figure is Roman.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

n4.text: The pose was popular in Roman times.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Imagine meeting this sleeper again in another museum, a little different each time.

q4.text: So is the Louvre's sleeper the one original?

choices.label: No: one of many Roman versions
No: it is a modern copy

correction.tempting: It is the most famous of them.
correction.truth: It is one of many Roman versions of the type, which differ in small details.
correction.evidence: Galleria Borghese, Rome; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

b4b.text: Yes. Many Roman versions of the sleeper survive, each a little different. What the first one looked like, and who made it, scholars still debate.

b4c.text: The figure is ancient, from Roman times.

correction.truth: Only the mattress, the pillow and some repairs are later. The sleeper is Roman.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

n5.text: In 1807 Prince Camillo Borghese sold it, and it went to Paris. It sleeps today in Room 348, on Floor 0 of the Sully wing.

lessons.takeaway: A Roman marble of Hermaphroditus, from Ovid's tale, who is both male and female: one of many Roman versions of the pose, laid in 1620 on a mattress carved by Bernini.
